19.1 · Social Networks

How Information Spreads Through a Network

If each person passes a message to just one other person, it crawls along a chain.

The same people, as they really are: about 300 people in 14 tight-knit communities, linked by a few long ties.

One person posts it. Everyone who sees it passes it to all of their contacts. Each band of color, from gold to violet, is one more degree of separation.

Hubs reach many people at once, and bridges carry the message into new communities. Nobody had to know more than a few people.

Click or press the clicker to step through.
19.1 · Social Networks and Degrees of Separation

Pass It On: How Influence Flows Through Networks

Social networks are systems of people and connections that allow money, information, influence, and even disease to flow, even between people who never interact directly. The two networks are built from this class: friend circles bridged one tie at a time (tight-knit) versus a network grown by preferential attachment, where a few people collect many ties (Barabási & Albert, Science, 1999). Colour shows degrees of separation from the person who started the message.

19.2 · Why Are Organizations Important for Change?

Scale, Reach, and the Power to Shift Systems

Nike, by 2016

After colleges criticized its waste generation, how much fabric waste could one company avoid?

2 million pounds
Nike reduced waste by 80% and avoided 2 million pounds of fabric waste by 2016.
That is the textiles 19,200 Americans throw away in a year.
= 100 people  ·  EPA: 17 million tons of textiles in U.S. trash in 2018

Organizations can act as nodes in vast social networks. Their decisions ripple outward through supply chains, customers, and communities.

A shift in manufacturing or purchasing policy at one large company can transform entire industries.

Organizational decisions move at a scale individuals cannot.

19.2 · The CSR Debate

Real or Greenwash?

Others warn of greenwashing: advertising sustainability while practicing the opposite. Here are three real claims. Which ones held up?

Volkswagen
Clean Diesel
“Our diesel cars meet strict U.S. emissions standards.”
EPA, 2015: software switched full emissions controls on only during tests. On the road, NOx ran up to 40 times the standard.
Patagonia
Our profits, for the planet
“Profits will go to fighting climate change and protecting land.”
In 2022 the founder moved ownership to a trust and a nonprofit, the Holdfast Collective, so profits fund climate and land work.
Ryanair
Lowest emissions
“Europe’s lowest emissions airline.”
UK Advertising Standards Authority, 2020: the ad was banned because the comparison wasn’t substantiated.
Judge all three ads Locked in. Watch the screen at the front.

EPA, Learn About Volkswagen Violations; Patagonia ownership announcement (2022); UK Advertising Standards Authority ruling on Ryanair (2020). Claims are paraphrased.

19.2 · Triple Bottom Line Accounting

People, Planet, and Profit

Figure 19.3. The three pillars of sustainability and their overlaps (after the widely used diagram, e.g. Adams, IUCN 2006). Click a circle. TBL coined by Elkington (1994).

Triple Bottom Line (TBL)

An accounting method that values social and environmental concerns alongside profits, rejecting the idea that financial returns are the only measure of organizational success.

19.3 · Mission Statement and Strategy

Whose Mission Is It?

Mission statements are shared internally and externally to build legitimacy. You know these brands. Which company wrote each one?

1“Saving people money so they can live better.”
2“To create a better everyday life for the many people.”
3“To organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible and useful.”
4“We’re in business to save our home planet.”
Match all four Locked in. Watch the screen at the front.
Mission Statement and Strategy
Mission statement

A brief, general value statement presenting an ideal vision of what an organization hopes to achieve, shared internally and externally to build legitimacy.

Strategy

How an organization directs its resources toward its goals. Walmart competes on cost; Apple on quality and brand. Sustainability initiatives succeed when they complement existing strategy.

Walmart purpose, corporate.walmart.com; IKEA vision, ikea.com; Google mission; Patagonia (the textbook figure in the “Mission and strategy” pop-up). A mission statement: a brief, general value statement presenting an ideal vision of what an organization hopes to achieve.

19.4 · How Can Members within an Organization Facilitate Change?

Change from Within

People lower in an organization’s hierarchy are often best-positioned to see problems and opportunities, and to initiate change.

Send an idea up from the bottom of the organization.

Professor David Orr at Oberlin College led the design and construction of the first green building at a US college in 1996, as a faculty member, not senior administration.

Figure 19.5b. The Adam Joseph Lewis Center, in use since its construction in 2000 (Oberlin College). Schematic elevation.

Figure 19.5a. A university as an organizational pyramid. Ideas often start at the base; whether they reach the top depends on support at each tier.

19.4 · Should Organizations Divest from Fossil Fuel Companies?

Vote with Our Dollars

  • Students at more than 100 colleges and universities have campaigned for divestment from fossil fuel industry stocks, directing institutional capital away from climate-damaging companies.
  • Divestment campaigns use financial pressure rather than protest, persuading institutions to sell stock in companies whose business model conflicts with stated values.

BRINGING IT TOGETHER

Change happens in networks, not in isolation.

  1. You are a node.Influence flows through ties. Hubs reach many people, and bridges carry new ideas between groups.
  2. Organizations are the hubs.One decision about what to make or buy ripples through supply chains, customers, and communities.
  3. Change comes from within.Mission, strategy, culture, and structure decide whether a good idea from anywhere in the hierarchy takes hold.
  4. And from outside.Consumers, media, nonprofits, investors, and partners press on organizations, and sustainability can pay.

Chapter 19 · Key Concepts

Groups & Organizations: How Do We Work Together for Sustainability?

Social Network
Systems of people and connections allowing information and influence to flow
Degrees of Separation
Measure of social distance between people in a network
Triple Bottom Line
Accounting for people, planet, and profit, not just financial returns
Corporate Social Responsibility
Expectation that companies adopt environmental and social goals
Greenwashing
Advertising environmental values while engaging in unsustainable practices
Benefit Corporation / B Corp
Legal status for businesses pursuing purposes beyond shareholder profit
Organizational Culture
Shared assumptions and behavioral patterns of group members
Divestment
Selling stock in companies whose practices conflict with stated values
